source.title: Why Larger Models Learn More: Effects of Capacity, Interference, and Rare-Task Retention
source.authors: Jing Huang; Daniel Wurgaft; Rachit Bansal; L. Ruis; Naomi Saphra; David Alvarez-Melis; Andrew Kyle Lampinen; Christopher Potts; E. Lubana

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present; there are minor text-extraction and formatting artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses published scaling-law forms as motivation for a phenomenological argument, but does not test those laws. Its experiments investigate rare-task learning and interference instead.
record.gate_note: The paper states power-law scaling equations and uses them to motivate its analysis, but does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute, fit extrapolation laws, or find compute-optimal allocations. It reports task-learning results in toy regressions and on injected OLMo tasks; the latter are trained during pretraining, so they are not downstream-task results as specified by V6. References to results from other work are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study uses published power-law and Chinchilla forms (α≈0.46, β≈0.51, γ=0.34 taken from Hoffmann et al.) only to motivate a phenomenological argument. It never fits or measures held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Its own results cover three things: per-task loss in a synthetic linear-regression mixture as width varies; injected-task accuracy and loss in OLMo 4M–4B runs; and representation and gradient analyses. The injected tasks are trained on during pretraining, so they are not downstream tasks as V6 means. The Appendix F results (task loss against C4 loss; task loss against compute) concern the injected task, not pretraining loss or allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. Smaller models lose a competition for capacity, so they fail to learn rare and complex tasks. Larger models learn them through reduced gradient interference and retention of rare-task updates. The authors offer this as a complementary, data-centric account, not a complete explanation of scaling, and note it was validated only at the tested OLMo scales.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurements. It uses theoretical analysis, synthetic multitask regression, and OLMo pretraining with controlled task injections to study rare-task learning and interference.
record.method_sensitivity: Task frequency, model width/size, task complexity, and the gap between injected task batches affect task-learning outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: In the OLMo injected-task runs, larger models learn lower-frequency injected tasks (comparison, modular addition) that smaller models fail to learn (Fig. 5). Larger models also show less gradient interference: non-task gradient cosine with the task direction is about 7.6e-5±0.02 at 1B versus 0.10±0.09 at 20M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With controlled injection during pretraining, the minimum model size needed to learn a task grows as the task's frequency falls.

fits_no_version.finding: Fig. 22 (App. F.1): at injected-task frequencies of 2.4e-6 to 2.4e-5, task loss tracks general C4 LM loss similarly across sizes. At 2.4e-7, larger models reach lower task loss at the same LM loss, and smaller models plateau.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For rare in-pretraining tasks, task loss is not a single function of general LM loss; it also depends on model size.

fits_no_version.finding: In the synthetic linear-bottleneck regression, per-task loss follows a utility ordering (πk·λk,j) as width grows. Tasks above capacity stay at the mean-predictor baseline even after 1M steps (Fig. 21).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a multi-task regression toy model, width determines which tasks are learned regardless of training length.

record.problems: The authors say empirical validation was limited to the tested OLMo scale and injected tasks, and does not establish behavior in larger-scale or over-trained language models or at extreme task frequencies. The aggregate task-performance outcome has no numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No individual model-by-frequency values are extracted from Figure 5; the text gives only the aggregate outcome recorded in R1. No results from cited studies are included.

untested.parts: Held-out LM pretraining loss versus N, D or C. No power-law fit is reported; the C4 validation loss in Fig. 22 is used only as an x-axis.
Extrapolation of small-run fits to larger runs.
Compute-optimal N and D allocation. Fig. 23 shows a compute frontier for injected-task loss only, with no fitted allocation exponents.
Effect of shape on loss at fixed parameter count. Only width is scaled; depth is fixed at 16, except 8 for the 4M model.
Other modalities or regimes. The synthetic regression mixture does not test a power-law form fitted to loss.
Downstream-task predictability from scale or pretraining loss. The injected tasks are part of the training data.
Dependence of fitted exponents or the compute-optimal split on setup and fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling-law exponents in Sec. 2 are quoted from Chinchilla, not measured here. Fig. 23's compute frontier uses 6ND compute against injected-task loss and does not bear on V3. No pretraining-loss scaling fits are reported, so no rows need adding for V1–V7.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation trends.
Effects of architecture details on held-out pretraining loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream-task performance predicted by scale or pretraining loss; the OLMo tasks here are injected during pretraining.
Dependence of scaling-law fits or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: OLMo models (4M to 4B; aggregate result as reported)
rows.stage_stated: pretraining on Dolma v1.7 with injected tasks
rows.operation_detail: Compared task learning across model sizes and controlled frequencies of injected comparison and modular-addition tasks.

conditions.value: varied across runs; exact tested values are shown in Figure 5

rows.measure: Injected-task test accuracy and training loss
rows.baseline: Smaller models at the same task frequency; exact baseline values not stated
rows.value: The paper reports that larger models learn lower-frequency tasks better, and that only larger models learn the infrequent and complex tasks; exact values are figure-only.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this aggregate outcome
rows.note: Aggregate result stated for the OLMo size sweep; the paper does not give per-model accuracy values in the text. This concerns injected-task learning, not any of V1–V7.
rows.check: The link to no version is correct. R1 measures injected-task accuracy and loss across OLMo sizes and task frequencies, not pretraining loss or a downstream task. Values appear only in Fig. 5 heatmaps. The subject is OLMo 4M, 20M, 300M, 1B and 4B, trained on up to 210B Dolma tokens.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Section 2 takes published power laws and exponents as premises rather than independently validating them.

tranche.reason: Uses published scaling-law forms to motivate its account of rare-task learning; its own results do not test V1–V7.

source_check.notes: Some row fields are ellipsized in the pack; the visible qualitative result matches Section 4.2. The authors' conclusion matches the discussion and limitations.
